History as a design constraint

How historical evidence becomes a playable system—and what is lost in the translation.

A historical strategy game makes an argument about how the world works. Its rules decide which resources matter, how institutions behave, and what kinds of choices are possible. These decisions deserve the same care as the visual representation of a period.

From evidence to rules

A useful starting point is to separate three things: what the sources establish, what the game engine can represent, and what a player needs to understand. Where those categories diverge, the design needs an explicit compromise.

A case from the project

To develop this note: choose one mechanic from Steam and Steel, identify its historical sources, explain the alternatives considered, and describe what testing revealed.

Open question

When does a simplification help someone understand the past, and when does it teach the wrong lesson?

Where processing ends and publishing begins

A short reading of the boundary between Meerkat’s pipeline and its reader-facing service.

Collecting an article and making it ready for readers are different operations. A pipeline can be midway through translation or analysis while the published collection still needs to remain usable and internally consistent.

Two kinds of state

The Meerkat architecture diagram distinguishes a pipeline schema from an app schema in PostgreSQL. Working data lives in the former; a full-state transaction publishes finished groups into the latter. The API reads the app schema.

Why the boundary matters

This arrangement makes publication an explicit step. It gives a clear place to reason about completeness and consistency, rather than treating every intermediate update as something a reader should immediately see.

To develop this note: add an example publication cycle, its failure cases, and the checks used before committing an update.

Keeping a useful project record

A small structure for documenting decisions while the reasons are still fresh.

A useful project note explains more than what changed. It records the problem, the constraints, the alternatives, and the evidence behind a decision. That context is often harder to reconstruct than the implementation itself.

A compact format

Begin with the question. Describe the smallest example that makes it concrete. Record the options considered and why one was chosen. End with what remains uncertain and what would justify revisiting the decision.

Evidence before polish

A diagram, a short comparison, or a link to a source can do more work than a long retrospective. The aim is to leave enough evidence for a future reader—including the author—to understand the reasoning.

To develop this note: include one actual decision from a current project and the evidence that changed its direction.
